description: ECG waveform profiles for cardiac conditions

profiles.name: Normal Sinus Rhythm
profiles.rhythm: Regular sinus rhythm with consistent P-QRS-T morphology
annotations: Normal P wave before every QRS

levelExplanations.explanation: This is a normal heart rhythm. The heart is beating regularly between 60-100 times per minute.
Normal sinus rhythm with upright P waves in II, regular rate 60-100, narrow QRS. Each P is followed by a QRS.
NSR with normal PR interval (120-200ms), narrow QRS (<120ms), normal QTc, no ST changes. Normal axis 0-90 degrees.
Normal sinus mechanism with intact AV conduction. Normal P wave morphology suggesting right atrial origin. Normal ventricular activation sequence.
Sinus node automaticity within normal range. Normal His-Purkinje conduction. No evidence of accessory pathways, conduction disease, or repolarization abnormalities.

profiles.name: Sinus Bradycardia
profiles.rhythm: Regular sinus rhythm at rate below 60 bpm

levelExplanations.explanation: The heart is beating slower than normal, less than 60 beats per minute. This can be normal in athletes or concerning if symptomatic.
Sinus bradycardia — rate <60 with normal P-QRS. Assess for symptoms: dizziness, syncope, hypotension. Consider atropine if symptomatic.
Sinus bradycardia may be physiologic (athletes, sleep) or pathologic (sick sinus, hypothyroidism, medications). Assess hemodynamic stability.
Evaluate for intrinsic sinus node dysfunction vs extrinsic causes (beta-blockers, CCBs, hypothyroidism). Holter monitoring for chronotropic incompetence.
EP study may reveal prolonged SNRT or CSNRT. If symptomatic and irreversible, pacemaker implantation indicated per ACC/AHA guidelines.

profiles.name: Sinus Tachycardia
profiles.rhythm: Regular sinus rhythm at rate above 100 bpm
annotations: P waves may merge with preceding T waves at high rates
Always look for the underlying cause

levelExplanations.explanation: The heart is beating faster than normal. This is usually a response to something else — pain, fever, dehydration, anxiety, or bleeding.
Sinus tach — treat the cause, not the rate. Pain, fever, hypovolemia, PE, sepsis. Rate usually 100-150.
Sinus tachycardia is a physiologic response. Differential includes hypovolemia, sepsis, PE, pain, thyrotoxicosis. Inappropriate sinus tachycardia is a separate entity.
May have rate-related ST depression (demand ischemia). Distinguish from SVT — sinus tach warms up and cools down, SVT starts/stops abruptly.
If persistent without clear cause, consider inappropriate sinus tachycardia or POTS. Ivabradine may be considered. EP study not usually indicated.

profiles.name: Atrial Fibrillation
profiles.rhythm: Irregularly irregular rhythm with no organized atrial activity
annotations: Assess for RVR vs controlled rate

levelExplanations.explanation: The top chambers of the heart are quivering instead of squeezing. The heartbeat is irregular — no pattern to it.
AFib: no P waves, irregular rhythm. Assess rate (RVR if >100). Key decisions: rate control, anticoagulation, cardioversion if unstable.
AFib with RVR: rate control with IV diltiazem or metoprolol. CHA2DS2-VASc for stroke risk. Cardiovert if hemodynamically unstable.
Classify as paroxysmal, persistent, or permanent. Echo for LAE and thrombus. Consider rhythm control strategy. TEE before cardioversion if >48hrs or unknown duration.
Pulmonary vein isolation ablation for drug-refractory symptomatic AF. LAA occlusion for anticoagulation-ineligible patients. Hybrid approaches for persistent AF.

profiles.name: Atrial Flutter
profiles.rhythm: Regular atrial activity at ~300 bpm with variable ventricular response
annotations: Sawtooth flutter waves best seen in II, III, aVF
Typical: 300 bpm atrial rate with 2:1 block = 150 bpm
Classic regular rate at 150 should prompt consideration of flutter

levelExplanations.explanation: A rapid, organized rhythm from the top of the heart. Usually very fast and regular. Look for a sawtooth pattern.
Atrial flutter at 150 bpm is classic 2:1 flutter. Sawtooth waves in inferior leads. Rate control and anticoagulation similar to AFib.
Typical flutter is a macro-reentrant circuit around the tricuspid annulus. 2:1 conduction gives rate ~150. AV blocking drugs may reveal flutter waves.
Distinguish typical (CTI-dependent) from atypical flutter. Adenosine can unmask flutter waves. Same stroke risk as AFib — anticoagulate similarly.
CTI ablation for typical flutter has >95% success rate. Atypical flutter requires detailed mapping. Often coexists with AFib — discuss combined ablation strategy.

profiles.name: Supraventricular Tachycardia
annotations: No visible P waves (or retrograde P in ST segment)

levelExplanations.explanation: A very fast, regular heartbeat usually between 150-250 bpm. The patient may feel palpitations, chest tightness, or dizziness.
SVT: regular narrow-complex tachycardia. Try vagal maneuvers first, then rapid push adenosine 6mg then 12mg. If unstable: synchronized cardioversion.
Most SVTs are AVNRT or AVRT. Regular narrow complex at 150-250. Adenosine is both diagnostic and therapeutic. If wide-complex, consider VT.
AVNRT shows pseudo-R in V1 and pseudo-S in inferior leads. AVRT may show short RP. Differentiating mechanism guides long-term therapy.
EP study with mapping and ablation. AVNRT: slow pathway modification (>95% success). AVRT: accessory pathway ablation. Consider for recurrent symptoms.

profiles.name: First-Degree AV Block
profiles.rhythm: Regular sinus rhythm with prolonged PR interval

levelExplanations.explanation: There is a longer-than-normal delay between the top and bottom chambers beating. Usually not dangerous.
First-degree AV block: PR > 200ms but every P wave conducts. Usually benign. Document and monitor.
Prolonged PR may be from AV nodal delay (drugs, vagal tone) or infranodal. Usually benign unless very prolonged or progressing.
If PR > 300ms, may cause pacemaker syndrome-like symptoms from AV dyssynchrony. Can be seen with digoxin, beta-blockers, CCBs.
Rarely requires pacing unless markedly prolonged with symptoms. His bundle recording can localize delay to AV node vs His-Purkinje.

profiles.name: Third-Degree (Complete) AV Block
profiles.rhythm: Complete AV dissociation with independent atrial and ventricular rhythms
annotations: P waves march through at their own rate
QRS at escape rate (junctional 40-60 or ventricular 20-40)
No relationship between P and QRS

levelExplanations.explanation: The electrical signal from the top of the heart cannot get through to the bottom. The bottom beats on its own, very slowly. This is dangerous.
Complete heart block: no conduction from atria to ventricles. P waves and QRS independent. Escape rate determines stability. Prepare for TCP/pacing.
Third-degree AV block: complete AV dissociation. Narrow escape = junctional (more stable). Wide escape = ventricular (less stable). Temporary pacing, then permanent pacer.
Causes include inferior MI (usually transient, nodal), anterior MI (usually permanent, infranodal), drugs, infiltrative disease, post-surgical.
Infranodal block requires permanent pacing. His bundle study differentiates level of block. Consider physiologic pacing (His bundle or LBBP) over RV apical.

profiles.name: Right Bundle Branch Block
profiles.rhythm: Regular sinus rhythm with wide QRS
annotations: Wide S wave in I and V6

levelExplanations.explanation: The electrical signal is delayed getting to the right side of the heart. This causes a wider-than-normal heartbeat on the monitor.
RBBB: wide QRS with RSR' in V1, wide S in I/V6. Can be normal variant or indicate right heart strain (PE, pulmonary HTN).
RBBB can be benign or pathologic. New RBBB with PE or RV strain is significant. Sgarbossa criteria modified for RBBB-STEMI diagnosis.
Isolated RBBB often benign. Combined with LAFB or LPFB suggests bifascicular block and more diffuse conduction disease.
HV interval prolongation in bifascicular block may indicate need for pacing. RBBB morphology VT suggests LV origin.

profiles.name: Left Bundle Branch Block
profiles.rhythm: Regular sinus rhythm with wide QRS
annotations: Broad notched R in I, aVL, V5-V6

levelExplanations.explanation: The electrical signal is delayed getting to the left side of the heart. This makes ECG interpretation harder. New LBBB can be a sign of heart attack.
LBBB: wide QRS, broad R in lateral leads, deep S in V1. New LBBB + chest pain = treat as STEMI equivalent. Use Sgarbossa criteria.
LBBB obscures standard STEMI criteria. Use modified Sgarbossa: concordant ST elevation >1mm or discordant >25% of QRS amplitude.
LBBB is often associated with structural heart disease (cardiomyopathy, aortic valve disease). Mechanical dyssynchrony may benefit from CRT.
CRT indicated for LBBB QRS >150ms with EF <35% and NYHA II-IV symptoms. His bundle pacing or LBBP as alternatives to traditional CRT.
This shows a heart attack affecting the front wall of the heart. The ECG lines are pushed up in certain spots. This is a life-threatening emergency.
Anterior STEMI: ST elevation V1-V4. LAD occlusion. Activate cath lab. Aspirin, heparin, NTG if no contraindication. Time is muscle.
Anterior STEMI from proximal LAD can affect large territory including septum and apex. Monitor for cardiogenic shock, VT/VF. Door-to-balloon <90 minutes.
Extensive anterior STEMI may cause severe LV dysfunction. Risk of mechanical complications (VSD, free wall rupture). Assess for multivessel disease at cath.
Primary PCI with DES. Consider mechanical support (IABP, Impella) for cardiogenic shock. Complete revascularization strategy for multivessel disease.

profiles.name: Inferior STEMI
profiles.rhythm: Sinus rhythm, may have bradycardia or AV block
annotations: Reciprocal depression in I and aVL
Check right-sided leads (V4R) for RV involvement

levelExplanations.explanation: This shows a heart attack affecting the bottom wall of the heart. The patient may also have a slow heart rate. This needs emergency treatment.
Inferior STEMI: ST elevation II, III, aVF. Usually RCA. Get right-sided ECG. Avoid NTG if RV involved. Watch for bradycardia and AV block.
Inferior MI from RCA (85%) or LCx (15%). RV involvement: hypotension, JVD, clear lungs. Treat with fluids, not NTG/diuretics. AV block usually transient.
ST elevation III > II suggests RCA culprit. ST depression V1-V3 may indicate posterior extension. Posterior MI: check V7-V9.
Primary PCI for RCA. RV branch occlusion may cause RV failure. Temporary pacing for high-grade AV block. AV block usually resolves within 1-2 weeks.

profiles.name: Monomorphic Ventricular Tachycardia
profiles.rhythm: Regular wide-complex tachycardia of ventricular origin

levelExplanations.explanation: A very fast, dangerous rhythm from the bottom of the heart. Wide complexes on the monitor. If pulseless, start CPR and defibrillate.
VT: wide complex regular tachycardia. Stable: amiodarone. Unstable: synchronized cardioversion. Pulseless: defibrillation + ACLS.
Monomorphic VT is usually reentrant around scar tissue. Amiodarone 150mg IV over 10 min for stable VT. Look for underlying ischemia or cardiomyopathy.
Brugada algorithm for WCT differentiation: AV dissociation, concordance, morphology criteria. Most WCT in structural heart disease is VT.
EP study with substrate mapping for VT ablation. ICD for secondary prevention. Scar-mediated VT: substrate modification with ablation. VT storm may require sedation/intubation and escalation.

profiles.name: Ventricular Fibrillation
profiles.rhythm: Chaotic ventricular activity with no organized rhythm

levelExplanations.explanation: The heart is quivering chaotically and not pumping blood. This is cardiac arrest. Start CPR immediately and use an AED/defibrillator.
VFib = pulseless = defibrillate immediately. CPR between shocks. Epi q3-5 min. Amiodarone 300mg after 3rd shock. Identify reversible causes (Hs and Ts).
VF is the most common initial rhythm in witnessed cardiac arrest. Early defibrillation is the most important determinant of survival. Double sequential defibrillation for refractory VF.
VF may be primary (ischemic) or secondary (electrolyte, drug-induced). Post-ROSC: targeted temperature management, coronary angiography, neuroprognostication.
Survivors of VF arrest without reversible cause need ICD. If recurrent VF (electrical storm), consider catheter ablation of triggering PVCs or VT.

profiles.name: Acute Pericarditis ECG
annotations: ST depression and PR elevation in aVR

levelExplanations.explanation: The lining around the heart is inflamed. The ECG shows changes in many leads at once, unlike a heart attack which shows changes in specific leads.
Pericarditis ECG: diffuse ST elevation, PR depression. Key differentiator from STEMI: diffuse changes, no reciprocal depression, concave ST morphology.
Four stages of pericarditis ECG: diffuse STE with PR depression → normalization → diffuse T inversion → normalization. Elevated troponin suggests myopericarditis.
Distinguish from early repolarization and STEMI. ST/T ratio > 0.25 in V6 suggests pericarditis. Echo for effusion. MRI if myocarditis suspected.
Recurrent pericarditis: colchicine + NSAIDs. Consider anakinra for refractory cases. Constrictive physiology: cath for hemodynamics, pericardiectomy if confirmed.

profiles.name: Wellens Pattern
profiles.rhythm: Normal sinus rhythm (pattern seen in pain-free interval)
annotations: Deep symmetric T wave inversions in V2-V3 (Type A)
Or biphasic T waves in V2-V3 (Type B)

levelExplanations.explanation: This pattern shows that a major heart blood vessel is critically narrowed. Even though the patient may feel fine right now, they are at very high risk for a heart attack.
Wellens syndrome: deep T inversions or biphasic T waves V2-V3 in a chest pain patient who is now pain-free. Critical proximal LAD. Do NOT stress test. Cath lab.
Two types: Type A (biphasic T waves, 25%) and Type B (deeply inverted symmetric T waves, 75%). Both indicate critical proximal LAD stenosis. Troponin may be normal or mildly elevated.
Wellens represents reperfusion T wave changes after transient LAD occlusion. High risk of anterior STEMI without intervention. Sensitivity and specificity >90% for proximal LAD disease.
Coronary angiography typically reveals critical proximal LAD stenosis. PCI with stenting is definitive treatment. Without intervention, 75% progress to anterior MI within weeks.

profiles.name: Paced Rhythm
profiles.rhythm: Regular paced rhythm with visible pacing spikes
annotations: Wide QRS (LBBB-like pattern for RV pacing)

levelExplanations.explanation: This person has a pacemaker. You can see small spikes on the ECG before each heartbeat. The pacemaker is telling the heart when to beat.
Paced rhythm: look for pacing spikes. Wide QRS with LBBB pattern from RV pacing. Verify capture (spike followed by QRS) and sensing.
RV apical pacing produces LBBB-like pattern. Failure to capture: spikes without QRS. Failure to sense: inappropriate spikes. Apply magnet for asynchronous mode.
Different pacing modalities: AAI, VVI, DDD, CRT. His bundle or LBBP pacing produces narrower QRS. Evaluate for pacemaker-mediated tachycardia.
Device interrogation for comprehensive assessment. His bundle pacing for more physiologic activation. LBBP as alternative to CRT in select patients.

profiles.name: Junctional Escape Rhythm
profiles.rhythm: Regular narrow-complex rhythm at junctional rate
annotations: No P waves or retrograde P waves

levelExplanations.explanation: The heart's backup pacemaker has taken over because the main one isn't working properly. The rate is slow but the rhythm is regular.
Junctional escape: narrow QRS, rate 40-60, no P waves. This is a rescue rhythm. Do NOT give anything that could suppress it. Consider atropine or pacing if symptomatic.
Junctional escape occurs when sinus node fails or complete AV block with junctional escape. More hemodynamically stable than ventricular escape due to normal activation sequence.
May be seen with digoxin toxicity, post-cardiac surgery, or inferior MI. Distinction from accelerated junctional rhythm (rate 60-100) important.
If persistent junctional escape from complete AV block, permanent pacemaker indicated. His bundle recording localizes block level.
